title: The pleasures of translating Plato
gist: Oxford classicist Armand D'Angour reviews the reissued Hamilton and Cairns Collected Dialogues of Plato (Princeton, 14 translators, 1961 pages), using examples to argue that every translation bears the stamp of its era and translator, and that technical arguments demand stricter fidelity than conversation.

insights.claim: The Hamilton and Cairns Collected Dialogues of Plato, first published by Princeton University Press in 1961 and reissued at £35, collects essentially all of Plato's writings in the work of 14 translators from Benjamin Jowett (1870s) to Hugh Tredennick (1954).
insights.speaker: Armand D'Angour
insights.so_what: Confirms the edition's continued commercial and scholarly relevance as a reference product.
insights.locator: The volume brought together readable English translations

insights.claim: The reissue has sturdier paper, semi-hard covers and a new foreword by Rebecca Newberger Goldstein, but the interior pages are reproduced from the original 1961 typesetting.
insights.speaker: Armand D'Angour
insights.so_what: Publisher is monetising a back-catalogue classic with minimal new editorial cost.
insights.locator: The volume now reappears in a new design

insights.claim: The collection is a period piece representing a Plato for the general English-speaking reader before 1961, with Jowett contributing seven of the translations, four more than any other translator, so its idiom often looks back to the Victorians.
insights.speaker: Armand D'Angour
insights.so_what: Readers should treat the edition as historically stamped rather than neutral.
insights.locator: Many of the versions Hamilton and Cairns chose

insights.claim: Every translation bears the stamp of its period and of its translator's taste, so there is no single neutral rendering of a Platonic text.
insights.speaker: Armand D'Angour
insights.so_what: Any text-based analysis built on a translation inherits that translator's biases; check the version used.
insights.quote: Every translation bears the stamp of its period and of its translator’s taste.
insights.locator: How far may a translator stray?

insights.claim: Opening the Republic, Plato's chosen word order puts katebēn ('I went down') first, evoking katabasis, the initiate's descent to the Underworld, a motif the Republic then plays out through the Cave and the tale of Er.
insights.speaker: Armand D'Angour
insights.so_what: Shows how structural meaning can sit in word order that translators may lose.
insights.locator: The Republic begins with four words

insights.claim: Translators differ even on small clauses: Shorey makes the Athenian procession the subject of both clauses, while Grube renders epichōrioi as 'local residents' and loosens the syntax, and a modern reader might prefer 'splendid' or 'a great show' over 'fine'.
insights.speaker: Armand D'Angour
insights.so_what: Illustrates concrete accuracy-versus-fluency trade-offs between editions.
insights.locator: A few lines after the opening of the Republic

insights.claim: Conversational passages give a translator room to manoeuvre, whereas technical passages and arguments turn on particular words and propositions, so the translator must stay close to the Greek or the logic does not survive.
insights.speaker: Armand D'Angour
insights.so_what: Rule of thumb: tolerate paraphrase in dialogue, demand literalness in argument.
insights.locator: Conversational passages in Plato leave a translator room

insights.claim: Michael Joyce's 1935 Symposium translation is expansive: it expands oiomenos ti poiein ('thinking I was achieving something') into 'firmly convinced that I was leading a full and interesting life', which is not necessarily worse than the author's own more concise version.
insights.speaker: Armand D'Angour
insights.so_what: Expansion can clarify tone but adds interpretation the original lacks.
insights.locator: The challenge is steep in the Symposium

insights.claim: Diotima's tokos en kalōi ('giving birth in beauty') binds physical procreation to the intellectual offspring of poets, lawgivers and philosophers, so kalon must be rendered by the same English term throughout, or the thread of the ascent from beautiful bodies to Beauty itself breaks.
insights.speaker: Armand D'Angour
insights.so_what: Illustrates how inconsistent term choice for elegance can destroy an argument's chain of reasoning.
insights.locator: When Diotima in the Symposium says

insights.claim: Alternating 'beautiful', 'fine' and 'noble' for stylistic elegance may read more easily but comes at the expense of breaking the thread of argument.
insights.speaker: Armand D'Angour
insights.so_what: Readability and analytical fidelity can conflict; prefer the latter for argument-heavy texts.

insights.claim: The edition's prefatory notes are still a useful guide and its remarkably full index lets readers trace a name, theme or term across dialogues, giving it enduring reference value.
insights.speaker: Armand D'Angour
insights.so_what: Apparatus, not only translation, sustains the longevity of the volume.
insights.locator: the prefatory notes are still a useful guide

insights.claim: The reissue is a reminder that earlier attempts to render Plato have not lost their value, and the treasury of Platonic thought can now be enjoyed in one handy volume by a new generation.
insights.speaker: Armand D'Angour
insights.so_what: Supports demand for classic humanities back-catalogue reissues.
